newsitem.title: UK: City of London awaits Labour moves on regulation.
newsitem.headline: City of London awaits Labour moves on regulation.

text.p: Britain's new Chancellor Gordon Brown may have given the Bank of England new direction but the City of London financial community remained in the dark on Tuesday on exactly how the new Labour government plans to regulate it.

Before its landslide election victory last week, Labour said it would merge top regulator the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) with the existing Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs). It also said it would reassess the bank's regulatory role.
"The interesting question is exactly how they do that," said a partner specialising in regulatory issues at a major accountancy firm here.
At present the SIB supervises the SROs, the so-called "frontline regulators" which authorise firms to conduct investment business, monitor them, handle complaints and punish rule breakers.
Regulatory responsibility has been divided between the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) and the Personal Investment Authority (PIA).

In the run up to the election Mike O'Brien, then Labour's shadow economic secretary, said his party would have to put in place a system flexible enough to adapt to market changes, characterising the current system as overly bureaucratic and expensive.
But since Labour's victory over the Conservative party, its leader Tony Blair has introduced a new face to take on the role of minister in charge of City regulation.

Helen Liddell, a 46-year-old who was one of Labour's shadow Scottish ministers, has been given the new role. But regulatory players said there was uncertainty as to the scope of her ministerial brief and what her approach will be.

"She's not really a known quantity in the way that Mike O'Brien was," said one regulatory source. O'Brien, who has been given a post in the Home Office, had shadowed the Conservative's Angela Knight in office for some time.
Apart from uncertainty over Liddell's approach to the City, questions have also been raised about the extent of the Bank of England's regulatory role.
The bank remains the watchdog for banks registered with it in Britain but came under criticism for its role in the collapse of British blue-blooded merchant bank Barings in February 1995.

Labour's new Chancellor of the Exchequer gave no indication of how the bank would fulfil its regulatory duties when announcing reforms to the bank on Tuesday, or how these would dovetail with the existing system, established under the Conservatives' Financial Services Act of 1986.

But the fact that Brown plans to appoint a second deputy governor of the bank was read in some quarters as an indication that its regulatory responsibilities would be enhanced, or at the very least would not be diminished.
"Not a lot has been said about the Bank of England. The message seems to be 'watch this space'," one banking source told Reuters.
Outside Britain the bank is well-known and well-respected and it would be a mistake to diminish or tamper with its role, he added.

Changes making the bank more independent will require legislation and if there is any change to the relationship between the self-regulatory bodies and the SIB, this might also need a change in the law, regulators said.
